sections.learningObjectives:
- Identify the core ethical principles of autonomy, beneficence, nonmaleficence, and justice and apply them to medical office situations.
- Recognize ethical dilemmas that arise when values or obligations conflict in the medical office.
- Apply office policy and supervisory guidance when handling privacy, confidentiality, and ethical questions within the assistant's scope of practice.
- Demonstrate professional conduct, including protecting patient information and staying within the supervised medical assistant role.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Autonomy is like being the boss of your own body and your own information: you get to choose, once you understand the choices.

### Question 2

Beneficence is like being a helpful teammate who actively does things to make things better for the other person.

### Question 3

Nonmaleficence is like being careful not to bump into someone while carrying a tray—your first job is to not hurt anyone.

### Question 4

Justice is like a referee calling the game the same way for both teams, no matter who is playing.

### Question 5

Autonomy means it is the patient's own information, so they get to look at it—like being able to read your own report card.

### Question 6

Keeping a secret safe so nobody gets hurt is like not telling the whole class something embarrassing about a friend.

### Question 7

Justice is like handing out the same number of crayons to every kid in class, no matter who they are.

### Question 8

Beneficence is like a teacher who stays after class to help a student understand the lesson because they want the student to succeed.

### Question 9

Covered entities are like the official teams that have to follow the privacy rulebook—doctors' offices, insurance plans, and clearinghouses.

### Question 10

The Notice of Privacy Practices is like the 'rules sheet' the office gives patients so they know how their private information will be handled.

### Question 11

Confidentiality is like whispering a friend's secret only where no one else can hear—you keep it private on purpose.

### Question 12

Minimum necessary is like pouring only the milk you need for one bowl of cereal instead of the whole carton.

### Question 13

Authorization is like a signed permission slip—the patient must say 'yes, you may share this' before the office hands their information to someone else.

### Question 14

A medical assistant is like a helper on a team who does important jobs, but the coach (the licensed provider) stays in charge.

### Question 15

If you are not sure you are allowed to do something, ask the person in charge before doing it—like checking with a teacher before using special equipment.

### Question 16

Being professional is like following the classroom rules and doing your job carefully and kindly, even when no one is watching.

### Question 17

A dilemma is like being asked to choose between two friends when both want you to pick them—neither choice feels completely right.

### Question 18

Amending a record is like being allowed to fix a mistake on your own homework that the teacher wrote down wrong.

### Question 19

This is like asking a friend to call your home phone instead of the family phone because you want privacy.

### Question 20

Some sharing is like the normal teamwork of a clinic—the doctor and billing staff can work together without a special permission slip every time.

### Question 21

If someone spreads a secret that embarrasses or hurts you, that is harm—so keeping the secret safe is a way of not hurting you.

### Question 22

Keeping a promise and following the rules at the same time—privacy is both a rule (law) and a promise (ethics).

### Question 23

Justice is like being equally friendly and helpful to every classmate, not just your best friends.

### Question 24

Beneficence is like a crossing guard who walks a younger student across the street—going out of the way to help.

### Question 25

Just because someone is family does not mean they get to see a patient's private results—the patient has to say yes first.

### Question 26

Looking at a patient's chart just because you are curious is like reading someone's private diary—it is not allowed, even if you keep it secret.

### Question 27

It is like leaving a note that says 'meet at 3 o'clock' instead of a long note with lots of private details.

### Question 28

There is a proper way to let someone else get your information—a signed permission slip—so the assistant should help set that up correctly.

### Question 29

A dilemma is like being told a secret that might help someone stay safe—you are torn between keeping the secret and protecting the person.

### Question 30

If your report card has a wrong grade, you can ask to have it fixed—patients can ask to fix mistakes in their own records too.

### Question 31

It is like packing only the clothes you need for a weekend trip instead of your whole closet.

### Question 32

This notice is like a 'how we use your information' card that patients are allowed to see and understand.

### Question 33

If someone is about to say something private out loud, you gently say 'let's talk somewhere private' instead of just letting it happen.

### Question 34

Sharing information so your own doctor can take care of you is like passing a note between your teachers—allowed without extra permission.

### Question 35

Before signing a permission slip, you should know exactly what you are saying yes to—like reading a field-trip form before signing it.

### Question 36

When two rules bump into each other and you are not sure what to do, you ask the adult in charge instead of guessing.

### Question 37

When someone official asks for private papers, you hand it to the person in charge to handle properly, not handle it yourself.

### Question 38

Your own health record is like your own report card—you are allowed to see it, with only a few special exceptions.

### Question 39

It is like asking a friend not to share something—they should listen, but they may not always be able to say yes.

### Question 40

If you mail a letter to the wrong house, you tell an adult right away so it can be fixed—you do not pretend it did not happen.

### Question 41

Autonomy is letting the patient be the captain of their own ship, with all the facts they need to steer.

### Question 42

If someone says 'please don't tell my family yet,' you keep that private—it is their choice to make.

### Question 43

You would not sign a paper you do not understand—so the assistant helps explain it first, like a teacher explaining a tricky question.

### Question 44

Justice is treating every customer in line the same way, no matter who they are or who they know.

### Question 45

Snooping in someone's private file is like reading their diary—it can hurt them, so it breaks the 'do no harm' rule.

### Question 46

Beneficence is like going the extra mile to help a friend study—you are actively doing something good for them.

### Question 47

It is like helping the person who is bleeding before the person who needs a bandage refill—help where it is needed most.

### Question 48

You can promise to keep a secret, but if the secret could help keep someone safe, you tell the grown-up in charge—not everyone.

### Question 49

When in doubt, look at the rulebook for your own team instead of making up a new rule on the spot.

### Question 50

Even saying 'yes, they have an appointment' is sharing private information, so the assistant keeps it private.

### Question 51

Using your private health info to advertise to you is a big deal, so it needs your signed permission.

### Question 52

If you find a spill, you tell the person in charge right away so it can be cleaned up—you do not just walk away.

### Question 53

The Privacy Rule is like a national set of rules to keep everyone's private health information safe.

### Question 54

Before sending something private to an email address, you make sure it is the right address and that the person asked for it.

### Question 55

Some decisions are only for the coach to make—the player helps but does not make the big calls.

### Question 56

If you hear someone sharing private information with a stranger, you step in or get help—you do not just let it keep happening.

### Question 57

Being told the rules before you choose is what lets you choose for yourself—like knowing the game rules before you decide to play.

### Question 58

It is only fair to explain the rules in a language the person can understand, not just in words they cannot read.

### Question 59

It is like asking for a list of who has seen your private information, so you can keep track.

### Question 60

If someone asks for one cookie, you hand them one cookie, not the whole jar.

### Question 61

If a friend says someone read their diary, you listen and help them tell an adult—you do not just say 'it is fine.'

### Question 62

Confidentiality is keeping a promise to keep someone's private information safe, like a lock on a diary.

### Question 63

If you are asked to use a tool you have not been trained on, you speak up and ask for help instead of risking an accident.

### Question 64

A dilemma is when two good rules clash—like keeping a promise versus keeping someone safe.

### Question 65

Justice is giving every person's request the same careful attention, like serving every customer in line fairly.

### Question 66

Before handing over private papers, you check who is asking and give only what they actually need.

### Question 67

It is the patient's own news to share, so they get to decide who hears it—like choosing who to tell about a big secret.

### Question 68

Just because someone is an emergency contact does not mean they get the private results—only the patient (or the law) can allow that.

### Question 69

If you find someone's private papers lying out, you pick them up and put them somewhere safe, then tell an adult.

### Question 70

Sending the whole binder when only one page was asked for is over-sharing—the opposite of 'just what is needed.'

### Question 71

A signed permission slip is still needed before handing over records—a spoken 'okay' is not enough.

### Question 72

Giving your best friend extra help while ignoring others is not fair—justice means everyone gets the same fair treatment.

### Question 73

The patient can ask for extra privacy, and the office must listen and follow its rules—but it cannot always promise yes.

### Question 74

Going out of your way to help someone understand so they can choose for themselves is the 'doing good' principle in action.

### Question 75

Never share your key or open a private file for someone who should not see it, even if they ask nicely.

### Question 76

A signature only counts if the person understood what they signed—if unsure, you stop and check with an adult first.

### Question 77

The law is like the minimum passing grade, but being a good person means doing more than the minimum.

### Question 78

When official legal papers arrive, you hand them to the person in charge to handle, not deal with them yourself.

### Question 79

If two rules clash and the rulebook does not tell you what to do, you go get the adult in charge.

### Question 80

When a big medical decision is the provider's job, the assistant points the patient to the provider instead of answering for them.

### Question 81

If you write something in the wrong notebook, you tell the teacher and fix it the right way—you do not erase it secretly.

### Question 82

It is like wanting to help a friend who says 'no thanks'—their right to choose bumps into your wish to help.

### Question 83

Everyone should be able to read their own information, so the office makes it work for each person—like providing a ramp as well as stairs.

### Question 84

If a folder contains someone else's secrets too, you do not hand over the whole folder—you let the person in charge decide what can be shared.
